extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy (Plato's Republic)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes Plato's prescriptive criteria for selecting and educating philosopher‑kings: the curriculum, stages/ages, personal qualities required, aims of the training, and warnings/anti‑patterns. Focus is on Books VI–VIII of the Republic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of education (from becoming to being)
rubrics_metrics.description: The true education is that which draws men from becoming to being, to a comprehensive survey of all being; it develops the faculty of seeing the universal in all things and leads the soul to the contemplation of the idea of good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education should not be mere useful information but a purification of the 'eye of the soul' so that particulars of sense drop away and the universal alone remains. The aim is both to 'realize abstractions' and to 'connect them' so that the student can combine universals into coherent knowledge (though the commentator notes Plato may overreach in assuming abstractions add to knowledge apart from facts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Curriculum sequence: mathematical prelude to dialectic
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical sciences form the prelude to dialectic: begin with number (arithmetic), then plane geometry, solid geometry (solids), solids in motion (including astronomy), and harmonics (music), and thence to dialectic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each branch is preparatory: number sharpens the mind and introduces contrast/relation; geometry compels the mind to look at true being; astronomy and harmonics should be pursued as abstract problems rather than mere sense‑observations. The sequence is intended to elevate the soul progressively toward dialectic, the 'royal road' out of the cave into the light.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetic/number as primary science
rubrics_metrics.description: Number or calculation is the universal or primary science of which all the arts and sciences partake; it conducts thought and being and is the first stimulant to intellect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arithmetic is to be regarded as pure abstraction (the unit is an absolute equality, not divisible) and valued for its power of sharpening the wits and testing general ability. Practical/military or retail uses may be retained but are secondary; arithmetic must be pursued 'in the spirit of a philosopher, not of a shopkeeper.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometry in stages (plane → solids → solids in motion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometry is the second branch: begin with plane geometry, then geometry of solids, and then solids in motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The geometer should pursue knowledge 'upwards to eternal existence' rather than downward to mere mechanical or artful applications; geometry's value is in elevating the soul and forming the mind of philosophy, though practical (military) uses exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Astronomy: abstract/problem-based study, not star-gazing
rubrics_metrics.description: Astronomy should be studied as problems and abstract dynamics rather than empirical 'star-gazing' or merely observing celestial appearances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato criticises contemporary astronomy for teaching the eye not the mind; the heavenly phenomena are imperfect copies and must not be relied on for true conceptions. Place astronomy on a truly scientific basis by problem‑solving and abstraction; its appeal is in drawing the soul upwards if rightly practised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonics/music as abstract harmony, not empirical auscultation
rubrics_metrics.description: Harmonics (theory of musical harmony) should be studied as the mathematics of unheard, true numerical relations, not by empirical ear‑tinkering or twisting strings to match pitch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Pythagorean approach (investigating numerical consonances) is closer to Plato's intention, but even that is incomplete if it stops at heard consonances; harmonics should be investigated in relation to the idea of the good and as part of universal knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialectic as the capstone (definer of essences and the good)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialectic is the science which defines and explains the essence or being of each nature, distinguishes and abstracts the good, and is the 'coping‑stone' of the sciences; it alone rises above hypotheses to first principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dialectic converts the mind out of opinion into intellect and is necessary to reach the idea of the good. It teaches to ask and answer questions, defend against opponents, and combine the sciences. It should follow mathematical training and is not to be revealed except to those disciplined in the prior studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection criteria for philosopher‑rulers (personal qualities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulers must be constant and valiant, good‑looking, of noble manners, possess natural ability improved by education, quick at learning, capable of mental toil, retentive, solid, diligent; they must combine intellectual with moral virtues and be sound in body and soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excluded are those 'lame and one‑sided' (diligent in body but indolent in mind or vice versa), 'a maimed soul' (hating falsehood but wallowing in ignorance), 'bastard or feeble' persons; candidates should be 'sound in wind and limb' and fit for rigorous mental gymnastic. Justice approves such natures as saviours of the State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age/stage timetable for training philosopher‑kings
rubrics_metrics.description: Educational stages and selection points: early childhood education in poetry/law/customs and gymnastic/music; first serious soul gymnastics in youth; selection at twenty of promising pupils; further selection at thirty for dialectic; after dialectic a period (roughly 5–6 years) followed by 15 years of practical experience (commanding armies, life experience); return at about fifty for philosophical leadership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested durations: second gymnastic training of the soul 'twice the time required for the gymnastics of the body' (five or six years commencing at thirty), then fifteen years practical service, and at fifty return to contemplation of the idea of good and potentially assume state leadership and train successors. Also an administrative measure: send out of the city all those more than ten years of age to expedite a generation's education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning against too‑early philosophical study for youth
rubrics_metrics.description: Young persons should not study philosophy too early; youth is 'a sort of puppy' who plays with arguments and can be 'reasoned into and out of' opinions, becoming unsettled and skeptical to their own and philosophy's discredit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophy studied too young can produce unsettled speculators who abandon former principles and become lawless or mere paradox‑lovers; wait until the sobriety of about thirty when argumentation becomes serious and steady. This is an anti‑pattern to avoid in educational design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attitude toward rule: rulers must not desire rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who rule must not be desirous to rule; the best‑fitted philosopher may be least inclined to rule, but necessity is laid upon him to descend into the den and rule for the common good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosopher‑kings should despise earthly vanities and serve justice only; they should be compelled (or accept) rule as a duty rather than personal ambition. This protects the State because rulers whose aim is political ambition are inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social arrangements: communal life and gender inclusion in guardianship
rubrics_metrics.description: In the perfect State wives and children are to be in common; the education and pursuits of men and women, both in war and peace, are to be common; women share in the same training and offices as men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guardians/soldiers live together, receive no pay beyond food from other citizens, and are to be warrior athletes and philosopher‑rulers; the ideal expects gender equality in capacities and civic duties (women will share in all things with men).
